reading_page.title: Energy Lab: The cell's energy budget
reading_page.text: A campus food-science team must decide whether cellular reactions can proceed. A negative Delta G indicates a thermodynamically favourable forward reaction, while ATP hydrolysis can drive an unfavourable step when the reactions are coupled and their Delta G values are added.

questions.question: Energy Lab: Which Delta G value describes a spontaneous reaction?
questions.explanation: A reaction is thermodynamically favourable or spontaneous in the forward direction when its Delta G is negative.
questions.similar_question: Which Delta G value describes a reaction at equilibrium?

questions.question: Why can ATP hydrolysis drive an endergonic biosynthetic reaction?
options: The summed Delta G of the coupled reactions can become negative
ATP changes every enzyme into a kinase
ATP removes all products from the cell
questions.answer: The summed Delta G of the coupled reactions can become negative
questions.explanation: When reactions are mechanistically coupled, their free-energy changes are added. A sufficiently negative Delta G for ATP hydrolysis can make the overall process favourable.
questions.similar_question: Why is ATP described as an energy currency rather than an energy creator?
similar_options: It transfers conserved chemical free energy between processes
It eliminates the first law of thermodynamics
questions.similar_correct_answer: It transfers conserved chemical free energy between processes

questions.question: A reaction with Delta G = +18.0 kJ/mol is coupled to ATP hydrolysis with Delta G = -30.5 kJ/mol. What is the combined Delta G?
questions.explanation: Delta G values are added: +18.0 + (-30.5) = -12.5 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is favourable.
questions.similar_question: Transport with Delta G = +22.0 kJ/mol is coupled to a reaction with Delta G = -28.0 kJ/mol. What is the net Delta G?

reading_page.title: Sprint Track: Glycolysis under pressure
reading_page.text: During a short, intense sprint, muscle needs ATP faster than oxygen delivery can support oxidative metabolism. Glycolysis invests ATP, splits six-carbon intermediates, and earns ATP in the payoff phase. When oxygen is limiting, lactate formation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

questions.question: Sprint Track: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP and produces 4 ATP, giving a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
questions.similar_question: How many pyruvate molecules are produced from one glucose during glycolysis?

questions.question: Which enzyme catalyses the first committed step of glycolysis?
questions.explanation: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and is a major regulated control point in glycolysis.
questions.similar_question: Which combination correctly describes regulation of PFK-1?
similar_options: Activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP
Activated by ATP and inhibited by AMP
Activated by citrate and inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
questions.similar_correct_answer: Activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP

questions.question: During oxygen-limited sprinting, why is pyruvate converted to lactate?
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase converts NADH to NAD+, allowing the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction and glycolysis to continue.
questions.similar_question: Why is lactate formation especially important for red blood cells?
similar_options: They lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP
They store large amounts of fat
questions.similar_correct_answer: They lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP

reading_page.title: Fuel Depot: Why glycogen is branched
reading_page.text: Liver and muscle store glucose as highly branched glycogen. Alpha(1->4) bonds form the chains and alpha(1->6) bonds form branch points. Many non-reducing ends allow several enzyme molecules to work at once, supporting rapid glucose-unit release.

questions.question: Fuel Depot: Which bonds form glycogen chains and branch points, respectively?
questions.explanation: Glucose residues in glycogen chains are linked by alpha(1->4) bonds, while branches are introduced through alpha(1->6) bonds.
questions.similar_question: Why do many non-reducing ends allow rapid glycogen mobilization?
similar_options: Many enzyme molecules can remove glucose units simultaneously
The ends release ATP without enzymes
questions.similar_correct_answer: Many enzyme molecules can remove glucose units simultaneously

questions.question: Why can liver glycogen support blood glucose while muscle glycogen mainly supplies muscle?
options: Liver contains glucose-6-phosphatase, whereas muscle lacks it
questions.answer: Liver contains glucose-6-phosphatase, whereas muscle lacks it
questions.explanation: Liver can hydrolyse glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose for release into blood. Muscle retains glucose-6-phosphate for local energy production.
questions.similar_question: Which enzyme converts glycogen-derived glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate?

questions.question: What is the most likely result of debranching-enzyme deficiency?
options: Glycogen with short outer branches accumulates
All glycogen is instantly converted to glucose
Glycogen becomes completely unbranched during synthesis
questions.answer: Glycogen with short outer branches accumulates
questions.explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase stops near branch points and cannot cleave alpha(1->6) bonds. The debranching enzyme is required for complete degradation.
questions.similar_question: What is the direct effect of muscle glycogen-phosphorylase deficiency?
similar_options: Reduced release of glucose-1-phosphate from alpha(1->4) bonds
Rapid conversion of fatty acids to glucose
questions.similar_correct_answer: Reduced release of glucose-1-phosphate from alpha(1->4) bonds

reading_page.title: Fasting Rescue: Rebuilding glucose
reading_page.text: As liver glycogen becomes limited during fasting, the liver synthesizes glucose from lactate, glycerol, pyruvate and glucogenic amino-acid carbon skeletons. Gluconeogenesis must bypass the three irreversible glycolytic reactions and consumes ATP, GTP and NADH.

questions.question: Fasting Rescue: Which set contains three gluconeogenic precursors?
questions.explanation: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids such as alanine can provide carbon for hepatic gluconeogenesis.
questions.similar_question: Which organ is the main site of gluconeogenesis during an overnight fast?

questions.question: Which enzyme bypasses PFK-1 during gluconeogenesis?
questions.explanation: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase hydrolyses fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate, bypassing the irreversible PFK-1 reaction.
questions.similar_question: Which enzymes together bypass pyruvate kinase during gluconeogenesis?

questions.question: What is required to synthesize one glucose from two pyruvate molecules?
questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis from two pyruvate consumes 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH per glucose molecule.
questions.similar_question: What is required to synthesize two glucose molecules from pyruvate?

reading_page.title: Control Room: Fed versus fasting signals
reading_page.text: A hepatocyte receives different instructions after a meal and during fasting. Insulin favours glucose use and storage. Glucagon activates cAMP and PKA, lowering hepatic fructose-2,6-bisphosphate so glycolysis slows while gluconeogenesis increases.

questions.question: Control Room: Which hormonal response is expected after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
options: Epinephrine suppresses glucose uptake in all tissues
questions.explanation: High blood glucose stimulates insulin, which promotes glucose uptake in responsive tissues and favours glycogen synthesis.
questions.similar_question: Which hormone promotes rapid glycogen breakdown during acute stress?

questions.question: What is the reciprocal effect of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?
options: It activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1
It inhibits both PFK-1 and FBPase-1
It activates FBPase-1 and inhibits PFK-1
questions.answer: It activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1
questions.explanation: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate stimulates glycolysis through PFK-1 and suppresses gluconeogenesis through inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
questions.similar_question: Why does low hepatic fructose-2,6-bisphosphate favour gluconeogenesis?
similar_options: PFK-1 loses activation and FBPase-1 loses inhibition
Both PFK-1 and FBPase-1 become permanently inactive
The pentose phosphate pathway stops producing NADPH
questions.similar_correct_answer: PFK-1 loses activation and FBPase-1 loses inhibition

questions.question: During fasting, glucagon activates PKA in liver. What is the expected metabolic outcome?
options: F2,6BP falls, glycolysis decreases and gluconeogenesis increases
F2,6BP rises, glycolysis increases and gluconeogenesis decreases
F2,6BP rises and both pathways increase equally
F2,6BP falls and glycogen synthesis increases
questions.answer: F2,6BP falls, glycolysis decreases and gluconeogenesis increases
questions.explanation: PKA phosphorylation favours the FBPase-2 activity of the hepatic bifunctional enzyme, lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and shifting metabolism toward gluconeogenesis.
questions.similar_question: What occurs when insulin promotes dephosphorylation of hepatic PFK-2/FBPase-2?

reading_page.title: Antioxidant Shield: The pentose phosphate pathway
reading_page.text: The oxidative pentose phosphate pathway produces NADPH and pentose phosphate. NADPH supports reductive biosynthesis and keeps glutathione reduced in red blood cells. Reversible non-oxidative reactions connect pentose phosphates with glycolytic intermediates.

questions.question: Antioxidant Shield: What are the major products of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway?
questions.explanation: The irreversible oxidative phase converts glucose-6-phosphate to ribulose-5-phosphate while generating two NADPH and releasing CO2.
questions.similar_question: Which glycolytic intermediates are connected to the reversible non-oxidative PPP?

questions.question: Why can glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency cause haemolysis after oxidant exposure?
options: Low NADPH limits regeneration of reduced glutathione
Low NADH prevents the CAC from releasing CO2
questions.answer: Low NADPH limits regeneration of reduced glutathione
questions.explanation: Reduced PPP flux lowers NADPH production. Glutathione reductase then cannot efficiently regenerate reduced glutathione, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative damage.
questions.similar_question: Which enzyme uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione?

reading_page.title: Carbon Roundabout: CAC and the glyoxylate bypass
reading_page.text: The citric acid cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA and loses carbon as CO2. Plants and many microorganisms can instead use the glyoxylate cycle, where isocitrate lyase and malate synthase bypass the carbon-losing reactions. Vertebrates lack this pathway and cannot obtain net glucose from even-chain fatty acids.

questions.question: Carbon Roundabout: What is produced during one turn of the CAC per acetyl-CoA?
questions.explanation: Each acetyl-CoA oxidized in the CAC yields three NADH, one FADH2, one GTP or ATP, and two CO2 molecules.
questions.similar_question: Which condition generally slows CAC flux?
similar_options: Increased substrate availability with low ATP

questions.question: Why can a germinating seed achieve net carbohydrate synthesis from acetyl-CoA?
options: The glyoxylate cycle bypasses the carbon-losing CAC steps
It converts acetyl-CoA directly to glucose in one reaction
It uses lactate dehydrogenase to make glycogen
questions.answer: The glyoxylate cycle bypasses the carbon-losing CAC steps
questions.explanation: Isocitrate lyase and malate synthase bypass the CAC decarboxylations, conserving acetyl-CoA carbon in four-carbon products that can support carbohydrate synthesis.
questions.similar_question: Which two enzymes are unique to the glyoxylate cycle?

questions.question: A fed liver has abundant glucose, high ATP, and needs fatty acids and nucleotides. Which carbon-flow plan is most appropriate?
options: Store glycogen, use PPP for NADPH and ribose, and supply citrate for fatty-acid synthesis
Activate gluconeogenesis and export all glucose
Convert all glucose to lactate and suppress the PPP
Use the glyoxylate cycle to convert fat into glucose
questions.answer: Store glycogen, use PPP for NADPH and ribose, and supply citrate for fatty-acid synthesis
questions.explanation: In the fed state, insulin favours glucose use and storage. The PPP supplies NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, while glycolytic carbon can provide citrate for fatty-acid synthesis.
questions.similar_question: Which plan best describes a fasting liver with active fatty-acid oxidation?
similar_options: Use glycogenolysis then gluconeogenesis; fatty-acid oxidation supplies energy but acetyl-CoA gives no net glucose
Activate glycogen synthesis and suppress gluconeogenesis
Convert acetyl-CoA to net glucose through the human glyoxylate cycle
Increase F2,6BP to maximise hepatic glycolysis
questions.similar_correct_answer: Use glycogenolysis then gluconeogenesis; fatty-acid oxidation supplies energy but acetyl-CoA gives no net glucose
